problemText: A transition in informative writing should name the relationship between two ideas. Which of these is NOT one of the seven transition families taught for informative paragraphs?
choices: Agreeing with the reader's personal opinion
Contrasting a real difference or exception
Adding one more fact on the same side
Showing cause and effect
hints: The seven families all describe how one fact connects to another fact in the text.
Look for the family that talks about connecting to something outside the paragraph.

problemText:
Read this pair of sentences from an informative paragraph about penguins: "Emperor penguins can dive deeper than 500 meters underwater to find fish. They hold their breath for up to 20 minutes during these deep dives." Which transition word would best fill the blank between these sentences?

Emperor penguins can dive deeper than 500 meters underwater to find fish. ___ they hold their breath for up to 20 minutes during these deep dives.
choices: However,
In addition,
For example,
Therefore,
hints: Ask yourself: does the second sentence turn against the first, explain why it happens, give one case of it, or add another fact about the same topic?
The second sentence gives you another separate fact about how deep penguins can dive.

problemText: A student is revising an informative paragraph about salt water and freshwater fish. The paragraph says: "Saltwater fish have special kidneys that help them get rid of extra salt. ___ freshwater fish have different kidneys that help them hold onto salt they need." Which transition correctly shows the relationship here?
choices: As a result,
Also,
However,
For instance,
hints: The two facts are about different types of fish with opposite kidney jobs. What kind of relationship is that?
One sentence is about saltwater fish, and the other is about freshwater fish—these are a real difference.

problemText:
Read this longer section from an informative paragraph: "Lightning forms when electrical charge builds up inside a cloud. ___ the negative charge at the bottom of the cloud pushes away negative charge on the ground below. ___ the ground becomes positively charged. ___ this imbalance finally releases as a lightning bolt that strikes upward from the ground to the cloud."

Which pair of transitions correctly fills the first two blanks in order?
choices: First, / However, / Finally,
However, / Also, / As a result,
For example, / Because, / In short,
In addition, / Therefore, / Next,
hints: The first blank comes after 'Lightning forms when charge builds up'—what does the next sentence do, add another cause or add another fact?
The second blank connects 'pushing away negative charge' to 'the ground becomes positively charged'—is one the result of the other?

problemText:
A student writes an informative paragraph about different types of owls and includes this sentence with a blank: "Great horned owls hunt small mammals like rabbits and mice. ___ barn owls also hunt small rodents, but they prefer to hunt in open grasslands instead of forests."

The student chooses the word "However" to fill the blank. Is this the correct transition? Explain why or why not based on what the two sentences actually say.
choices: No, because the second sentence adds a new fact about barn owls rather than turning against what was said about great horned owls.
Yes, because the second sentence contradicts the first by showing that barn owls hunt in a completely different way and location, making "however" show the contrast between the two owl species.
Yes, because "however" is a polite, grown-up word that works in informative writing and sounds professional when explaining facts about animals.
No, because "however" is used only to show the order that events happen in, and these sentences describe the hunting habits of different owls rather than events in time sequence.
hints: Does the second sentence disagree with or contradict the first sentence, or does it give one more fact on the same side?
Remember: a transition can sound right and still name the wrong relationship—check what the second sentence actually does to the first fact.

problemText:
A student revises an informative paragraph about bird migration and reads it aloud: "Many bird species migrate to warmer places in the fall. Similarly, monarch butterflies fly south to escape the cold. However, some birds migrate to find food rather than warmth. Therefore, the path a migrating animal takes depends on what resources it is looking for."

Which sentence has a transition that names the wrong relationship, and what is the actual relationship that sentence shows?
choices: Sentence 2: 'Similarly' names the adding relationship, but the sentence actually shows an example relationship.
Sentence 3: 'However' names the contrast relationship, but the sentence actually adds a separate cause for migration.
Sentence 4: 'Therefore' names the cause-and-effect relationship, but the sentence actually concludes the paragraph.
No sentence has the wrong transition; all four transitions correctly name their relationships.
hints: Read each sentence before and after the transition, and ask: does the relationship the transition announces match what the sentence actually does?
Look especially at sentence 3. It gives one more reason why animals migrate—is that turning against the migration-for-warmth idea, or adding to it?

problemText: A concrete detail is one of the ways to develop a topic sentence. Which choice is the best example of a concrete detail that develops a topic?
choices: The cafeteria serves vegetables because the school believes that including healthy food options supports student nutrition and overall wellness.
The cafeteria includes vegetables at lunch because they provide important nutritional benefits and promote good health in students who eat them regularly.
The cafeteria is a pleasant space where students can gather to eat lunch together with their friends and enjoy their meals in a comfortable setting.
The school cafeteria serves many different kinds of vegetables, including carrots, broccoli, green beans, and cauliflower on Monday through Thursday.
hints: A concrete detail names specific, exact things—like numbers, names, or particular actions—not just general feelings.
Which choice lets a reader actually picture what vegetables are served and when?

problemText: Read this topic sentence: "Dogs use their sense of smell to understand the world around them." Which sentence actually develops this topic by adding new information instead of just restating it?
choices: A dog's nose has millions of scent receptors, and when a dog sniffs the ground, it can tell how old a scent is, what direction an animal traveled, and whether the animal was injured or afraid.
Dogs are able to use their sense of smell effectively in many different daily situations because it helps them gather information that is useful for survival and understanding their surroundings.
Dogs are known for being intelligent animals with many special abilities that make them valuable helpers for humans in a variety of jobs and situations.
The sense of smell is important for dogs because it is one of several ways they gather information and learn about what is happening in the world around them each day.
hints: Test each sentence against the topic sentence: Does it tell the reader something new, or does it just repeat the same idea in different words?
The correct answer explains specific, checkable things that happen when a dog sniffs—not just that the sense of smell is good.

problemText: A student wrote this topic sentence: "Rainforests are disappearing quickly." Then the student added this sentence: "Rainforests are important ecosystems with many plants and animals." Why does this sentence NOT develop the topic?
choices: It introduces new information about rainforests but does not connect that information to the topic of how quickly they are disappearing.
It is about rainforests in general, but it does not explain the specific topic—how fast they are disappearing or why.
It includes the word 'ecosystems,' which is a technical term that most readers may not understand without further explanation.
It fails to mention specific rainforests like the Amazon or the Congo, which would make the sentence more concrete and convincing.
hints: Remember the relevance test: A fact can be true about the general subject but still fail to develop the specific topic sentence.
The topic sentence is about disappearing quickly. Does the sentence added explain anything about speed or loss?

problemText: Read this topic sentence: "Monarch butterflies make an amazing journey that takes several generations." A student wants to develop this topic by adding facts and details. Which pair of sentences best develops the topic by avoiding restatement and staying specific to this exact topic?
choices: These sentences use general language about butterfly behavior that could apply to many different butterfly species, but they do not show exactly how the monarch's journey requires several generations or explain what each generation contributes to the overall migration.

These sentences describe migration as a common behavior found in many insect species and animals, but they do not specify how the monarch's specific journey requires multiple generations to complete or explain why each generation lives a different amount of time.

A single monarch butterfly cannot live long enough to complete the entire round-trip journey between Canada and Mexico. Instead, the fall generation that hatches in late summer lives several months and flies south, then spring generations born during the return journey each live only a few weeks before passing the journey to the next generation.

These sentences describe the monarch migration as an impressive or wonderful natural event, but they do not provide concrete facts about how the generations are involved or explain in detail how the multi-generational cycle actually functions during the journey.
hints: Look for sentences that explain a specific, checkable fact about the monarch's journey itself—not just general praise for how 'amazing' it is.
Which choice shows how the journey takes multiple generations by describing what actually happens in each generation?

problemText: A writer wrote this topic sentence: "The Great Wall of China was built over many centuries to protect against invasions." Then the writer added: "Thousands of workers built the wall, and it required a huge amount of stone." Identify what is wrong with the added sentence and explain why it fails to properly develop the topic.
choices: The sentence uses approximate language like 'thousands' when it should state a precise count of workers from historical records.
The sentence brings up multiple separate facts about workers and stone, but neither one explains how the centuries of construction occurred or describes the defensive strategy against invasions.
The sentence introduces new topics about workers and building materials that shift focus away from the main idea about China as a nation.
The sentence restates that the wall was built but does not explain how the centuries-long construction or the defense strategy actually worked.
hints: Run the relevance test: Does this sentence explain something new about the centuries-long building process or how the wall protected against invasions, or does it just repeat that it was built?
The topic sentence mentions two specific ideas: built over centuries and protected against invasions. Does the added sentence develop either of those ideas?

problemText: A student wrote: "Mountain lions are dangerous predators." Then added three sentences: (1) "Mountain lions are scary animals that can hurt people." (2) "A mountain lion hunted a family's pet dog near the edge of their neighborhood on the outskirts of Denver, Colorado in 2019, dragging it away into the forest." (3) "These big cats live in many different areas and eat meat for survival." Identify which sentence properly develops the topic and explain why the others do not, based on the rules for facts, details, and relevance.
choices: Sentence 2 develops the topic because it gives a concrete, specific example of the danger with a real place, time, and action that readers can picture and verify, whereas Sentence 1 only restates the topic and Sentence 3 states a general fact about mountain lions that does not explain the specific topic of danger.
Sentence 1 develops the topic because it uses vivid and emotionally descriptive words such as 'scary' to emphasize how dangerous and threatening mountain lions truly are to people.
Sentence 3 develops the topic because it provides an explanation of why mountain lions hunt other animals, demonstrating that they are predators who need meat to survive and therefore pose a danger.

Sentence 2 develops the topic because it focuses on the attack against a pet dog rather than a human victim, making it a more detailed and interesting example of the mountain lion's predatory behavior.
hints: Apply three tests: Does it restate the topic without adding new information? Does it state a general truth about the subject but not about this specific topic? Does it give a concrete, checkable example or detail?
Which sentence shows an actual instance of danger happening, with specific details about where, when, and what the mountain lion did?

problemText: A writer is planning an informative piece about the school's new tardy policy. She has gathered that the policy applies to students who arrive after 8:15 a.m., that the first tardy results in a warning, that a second tardy means staying after school for 15 minutes, and that a third tardy means a phone call home. Which organizing strategy fits this information best?
choices: Comparison/contrast strategy, because it weighs the tardy policy against other school policies.
Classification strategy, because it sorts the policy into different types of consequences based on how many tardies a student has.
Definition strategy, because it explains what a tardy is and describes its key features one at a time.
Cause/effect strategy, because it explains why students arrive late to school.
hints: Think about what kind of information the writer gathered—is she explaining what something is, sorting it into groups, comparing two things, or explaining why something happens?
The notes describe the tardy policy's key features (what counts as a tardy, what the rule is) rather than splitting it into categories or comparing it to something else.

problemText: A student is drafting a paragraph about the school library's books using the classification strategy. Which opening sentence best signals that the paragraph will sort books into groups?
choices: The school library has many different types of books, and they are separated based on what subject matter and format each one contains.
The oldest book in the school library was published in 1998, while the newest book arrived last month and is very popular.
Books in the school library are important resources because they help students learn new information and develop their ideas.
The school library organizes its books into four main sections: fiction, nonfiction, graphic novels, and reference books.
hints: Look for an opening sentence that names the topic and announces that groups or kinds are coming next.
Classification sorts a topic into types or categories, so the opening should introduce those categories by name.

problemText: A writer has gathered these notes about two lunch options: the hot lunch line serves warm food and has a wait of about 10 minutes; the cold lunch option offers sandwiches and fruit already on display and takes 2 minutes to grab. The writer wants to organize an informative piece using the comparison/contrast strategy. Which statement about how this piece should be organized is correct?
choices: The piece should describe both lunch options side by side, explaining how they are alike and different across the same categories.
The piece should explain why some students prefer hot lunches more than others prefer cold lunches based on taste and convenience factors.
The piece should describe only the hot lunch line in detail first, then briefly mention what makes the cold lunch option stand out as different.
The piece should sort all lunch options in the cafeteria into groups such as hot foods, cold foods, drinks, and desserts.
hints: Comparison/contrast strategy is built for exactly two named things, not one or more than two.
When using comparison/contrast, a writer describes both things using the same categories so the reader can see how they match up.

problemText:
A student drafted this paragraph about why recess ends early on rainy days, using the cause/effect strategy. Read the four sentences carefully.

(1) When it rains, water makes the playground slippery and unsafe for running games. (2) The gym class that normally goes outside comes inside to the gymnasium instead. (3) Teachers worry that a student might slip and get hurt on wet grass or muddy areas. (4) The school's playground equipment is made of metal and plastic, while the gym equipment is made of rubber and foam.

Which sentence breaks the one-strategy rule for this paragraph, and why?
choices: Sentence 1, because it describes the playground instead of explaining a chain of cause and effect.
Sentence 4, because it compares two types of equipment instead of continuing the chain of cause and effect.
Sentence 3, because it explains a reason why something happens, which fits the cause/effect strategy.
Sentence 2, because it names what happens as a result, which continues the cause/effect chain correctly.
hints: Look for a sentence that switches from explaining why or what happens as a result (cause/effect) to a different organizing idea.
Cause/effect is about chains of why and what-happens-next, not about weighing one thing against another thing.

problemText: A student has gathered information about after-school clubs: the Art Club meets on Mondays and teaches drawing and painting; the Science Club meets on Wednesdays and does experiments; the Art Club costs $20 for the whole year; the Science Club costs $15 for the whole year. The student wants to write an informative paragraph but is unsure which strategy to use. Which strategy would work better for this information, and why?
choices: Definition strategy, because the student needs to explain what after-school clubs are and then describe how each one operates throughout the academic year.
Classification strategy, because the student needs to sort multiple clubs into groups based on whether they focus on arts or sciences and their price ranges.
Comparison/contrast strategy, because the information describes two named clubs across the same categories, so they can be weighed side by side.
Cause/effect strategy, because the information shows why the Art Club and Science Club meet on different days and have different costs.
hints: The student has gathered information about exactly two clubs, not three or more, and described them using the same categories.
Notice which strategy is built for setting two specific named things alongside each other to show how they are alike and different.

problemText:
A student wrote this paragraph about the types of homework assignments students receive:

"Homework assignments fall into three types: worksheets, which students complete at home and turn in the next day; projects, which students work on over several days and present to the class; and reading, which students finish before class starts. Worksheets help students practice skills they learned in class. Projects take more time than worksheets, so teachers give fewer of them. Reading assignments build vocabulary and understanding."

Identify which sentence breaks the one-strategy rule, explain why it breaks the rule, and describe what the strategy should be to fix the paragraph.
choices: The sentence 'Homework assignments fall into three types' breaks the rule because it names the strategy and should be replaced with a sentence that introduces the first type of homework without announcing the overall framework.

The sentence 'Worksheets help students practice skills they learned in class' breaks the rule because it explains the purpose of worksheets rather than simply describing what they are and when they are due.

The sentence 'Reading assignments build vocabulary and understanding' breaks the rule because it states a benefit instead of describing what reading assignments are and how long students have to complete them.

The sentence 'Projects take more time than worksheets, so teachers give fewer of them' breaks the rule because it compares two types instead of naming a group; remove it and replace it with a sentence that describes projects as a group.
hints: The paragraph opens with classification, naming three types of homework, so every sentence after that should describe one type or say something true about each type.
Look for a sentence that suddenly switches to a different job—comparing, explaining why, or weighing one group against another—instead of staying inside the classification strategy.

problemText: A narrative opening needs to answer three questions before the first event finishes. Which of the following is one of those three questions an opening must answer to orient a reader?
choices: What will happen at the very end of the story?
Where and when is this happening?
How does the main character feel about everything that occurs?
What did the characters do before this story began?
hints: Think about what a reader needs to picture right away to understand where they are standing.
The three jobs of an opening are about context, a character or narrator, and the first event—not about the ending or distant past.

problemText: A writer wants to open a story about a soccer player who discovers her uniform is missing on game day. The writer drafts this opening: "Keisha had been playing soccer since she was five years old. Her family always came to her games. She loved being on the team." Why does this opening fail to orient a reader properly, even though it introduces a character?
choices: It does not tell the reader how the story will end or what problem the character will face.
It mentions Keisha's family and her past experiences rather than showing her facing a challenge in a specific moment and place.
It lists facts about Keisha instead of showing her doing something right then, and it does not establish where or when the story is happening.
It focuses on Keisha's history and feelings over time rather than grounding the reader in a specific setting and showing what Keisha is doing at the moment the story begins.
hints: Look at what the writer tells us about Keisha—is it information about her past, or something she is doing right now in a place we can picture?
Remember that orienting means naming a character AND giving a reason that person is there right then, not describing their history.

problemText: A writer opens a story this way: "It was Tuesday morning in the art studio when Devon noticed the pottery wheel was broken. He reached for the clay jar but stopped when he saw the crack running across the wheel's base." Does this opening orient the reader properly? Why or why not?
choices: No. It describes Devon noticing something instead of showing him making a decision or taking action.
Yes. It names the art studio and mentions clay, so a reader knows exactly what kind of art Devon does.
No. It only tells the day of the week and time of day without describing what the studio looks like or why Devon is there.
Yes. It tells the reader where and when the story is taking place, introduces Devon by name, and stops at the first event that starts the story moving.
hints: Check whether the opening answers the three questions: where and when, who is there, and what happens first.
The first event is the moment that gets the story moving—does this opening stop there, or does it race ahead to later events?

problemText: A writer starts a story with this sentence: "Ramon was sitting on the curb outside the grocery store on a Saturday morning when the delivery truck pulled up and hit a stack of watermelons, and watermelons rolled everywhere, and customers stopped to pick them up, and the manager came out and apologized to the driver." This opening has both context and a character, but why does it fail as an orienting opening?
choices: It races through too many events instead of stopping at the first event, making it sound like a summary rather than an opening.
It does not include any concrete details about what the grocery store looks like or describe the size and color of the watermelons.
It does not name the character by his first name clearly enough or explain his full background.
It does not explain why Ramon was sitting on the curb or what he was planning to do there.
hints: An orienting opening should stop once the first event happens—the moment that starts the story moving. Does this sentence stop there, or does it keep going?
Think about the difference between starting a story and summarizing what happens in it. This sentence does which one?

problemText: Two writers are opening stories. Writer A writes: "Lily was at her grandmother's house in the kitchen on a sunny afternoon when the timer on the oven went off, and she opened the door, and the cookies had burned, and she felt terrible about it." Writer B writes: "Lily was at her grandmother's kitchen on a sunny afternoon when the oven timer suddenly went off. She pulled open the door and froze." Which opening better orients a reader without giving away what happens, and what makes it better?
choices: Writer A's opening is better because it tells the reader everything that happens in the story so nothing is left unanswered or confusing.
Writer B's opening is better because it establishes the context and introduces Lily, but stops right when the first event begins, letting the reader wonder what she sees when she opens the door.
Writer A's opening is better because it connects all the events together in one long sentence, which shows how they are related to each other.
Writer B's opening is better because it uses simpler words and shorter sentences than Writer A, making it easier for readers to follow.
hints: An orienting opening should not give away the ending or the middle of the story. Which opening tells too much already?
A natural sequence starts at the first event and lets readers experience what happens next—which opening does that?

problemText: A writer has three possible opening sentences for a story about a student who loses an important library book. Sentence 1: "Jamal had checked out the book three weeks earlier, and he had read half of it, and then he could not find it anywhere, and he had to pay a replacement fee, and he was upset about it for weeks." Sentence 2: "Jamal was searching through his backpack in the library parking lot on Thursday afternoon when he realized the book he needed to return before fifth period was no longer in any of the pockets." Sentence 3: "A student named Jamal once lost a book from the library." Which opening best orients the reader, and why? Consider what the three jobs of an opening are and which sentence accomplishes all three without rushing ahead or stalling.
choices: Sentence 3, because it is the shortest and clearest introduction of the character without any extra details that might confuse the reader.
Sentence 1, because it gives the reader all of the details about what will happen in the story and how long the conflict lasts, so there are no surprises.

Sentence 2, because it establishes a specific time and place, introduces Jamal by name and tells what he is doing right then, and stops at the first moment of trouble instead of reporting the whole chain of events or just stating a fact.
Sentence 3, if written with more details about why Jamal lost the book and when he discovered it was gone.
hints: Check each sentence against the three orienting jobs: Does it say where and when? Does it name a character and show what that person is doing right then? Does it stop at the true first event?
Which sentence gives away too much of the story before a reader has anything to care about, and which one just tells a fact without any context or action at all?
